title: You didn’t fall because you were weak.
paragraphs: You didn’t fall because you were weak.
You drifted because you were busy.
That’s the part no one warns you about.

You didn’t wake up one day and decide to walk away from God. You just had things to do. Responsibilities. Deadlines. Messages to answer. People to please. And somewhere in the middle of all that movement… your soul went quiet.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Distraction is one of the enemy’s most effective weapons—not because it looks evil, but because it looks necessary.
Luke writes about a moment that feels uncomfortably familiar:
“But Martha was distracted with much serving…” (Luke 10:40)
Not rebellious. Not sinful on the surface. Not immoral.
She was serving. Doing something good. Something honorable. Something that probably needed to be done. Yet Jesus didn’t commend her for it.
Because what pulled her away from Him didn’t look like destruction.
And that’s where it gets dangerous.
Because you can be doing good things… and still be drifting from the only thing that gives you life.

You felt it in those quiet moments when the noise faded and something inside you whispered, “This isn’t enough.” You tried to silence it with more activity. More scrolling. More work. More distractions.
Because your soul wasn’t created to run on productivity.
She was wrong for letting service replace surrender.
That’s why Jesus answered her in a way that cuts through centuries and lands directly on you:
“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary…” (Luke 10:41–42)
And you’ve been giving your life to everything except that.
This is how people slowly lose intimacy with God—not through open rebellion, but through quiet neglect.
And eventually… His voice feels distant.
But because you filled every space where He used to speak.
You didn’t mean to replace Him.
And the enemy doesn’t need to drag you into darkness if he can keep you too preoccupied to notice you’re already drifting.
He doesn’t need to destroy your faith.
He just needs to dilute your focus.
Because a distracted believer is a powerless believer.
And deep down, you know it.
And distance always grows where attention disappears.
But this is where everything turns.
Because Jesus didn’t just expose Martha.
He pointed to Mary—sitting at His feet, listening, present, undistracted—and said she had chosen “what is better.”
And here’s the Gospel that changes everything:
You don’t have to earn your way back into that place.
You don’t fix distraction by trying harder.
“Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10)
Because your greatest need isn’t to get more done.
It’s to come back to the One you’ve been too busy to sit with.
And Jesus already made the way.
“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28)
The cross didn’t just save you from sin.
So now you’re standing in a moment that matters more than you think.
You can go back to the noise.
Or you can finally slow down long enough to hear Him again.
And you already know which one your soul is desperate for.
Let it expose what you’ve been avoiding.
Say it plainly if you feel it:
If you know someone who’s been drowning in busyness, send this to them. They won’t say it out loud—but they feel it.
You’ll need the reminder again when life gets loud.
There’s more waiting for you than surface-level faith.
